lessons.focus: Quotations, paraphrasing, summarising and avoiding over-quoting

data.title: Using Evidence
data.summary: In this lesson students learn how to use quotations, paraphrase, and summarise sources effectively, and understand why over‑quoting weakens an essay. They will also see practical steps to integrate evidence without relying too heavily on direct quotes.
objectives: Identify when to quote, paraphrase, or summarise a source
Rewrite a passage in their own words while keeping the original meaning
Create a concise summary of a longer text
Avoid over‑quoting by balancing their own voice with evidence
data.prerequisites: Students should already know the basics of essay structure and why evidence is needed in academic writing.
why: Using evidence correctly shows that you understand the material and can support your arguments, which is essential for success in school, university, and many jobs that require clear communication.
Avoiding over‑quoting helps you develop your own voice and critical thinking skills, making your writing more persuasive and trustworthy.

sections.heading: Why Use Different Types of Evidence?
sections.body:
When you write an essay or a report, you are not only showing what you think, but also showing that your ideas are backed up by reliable information.  
The way you bring that information into your own writing can be done in three main ways: **quoting**, **paraphrasing**, and **summarising**. Each method has a purpose, and using the right one at the right time makes your argument clearer and more convincing.

First, think of evidence as pieces of a puzzle. A quotation is a single piece that fits perfectly because it is exactly the shape the original author gave you. You keep the piece unchanged, so the picture on it is exactly the same as in the original picture.  
> **Definition:** *Quotation* – copying the exact words of a source, enclosed in quotation marks and followed by a citation.

A quotation is most useful when the original wording is especially powerful, memorable, or authoritative. For example, if Martin Luther King Jr. said, “I have a dream that one day…”, you would quote those words because the phrasing itself carries a strong emotional weight that would be lost if you changed it.

Second, a paraphrase is like taking a puzzle piece, looking at its shape, and then carving a new piece that fits the same spot but matches the style of the rest of your puzzle. You keep the original idea, but you express it with your own words.  
> **Note:** *Paraphrasing* means restating a source’s idea in a different way while keeping the meaning the same, and you must still give credit to the original author.

Paraphrasing is handy when the idea is important, but the exact wording is not critical. It also shows that you understand the material well enough to explain it yourself. For instance, instead of quoting a long definition of “photosynthesis,” you might write: *Plants turn sunlight into food through a process called photosynthesis.* This keeps the flow of your essay smooth while still acknowledging the source.

Third, a summary is like looking at several puzzle pieces together and drawing a quick sketch that captures the overall picture. You condense a larger section of text—sometimes a whole article—into a few sentences that convey the main points.  
> **In daily life:** *Summarising* is like telling a friend the plot of a movie you just watched, without describing every scene.

Summaries are useful when you need to give background information or show the broader context of a debate without getting bogged down in details. If you are writing about climate change, you might summarise a 20‑page report by stating: *The report concludes that human activities are the primary driver of recent global warming.* This gives readers the essential conclusion while leaving the detailed data for later reference.

Why mix these three? Imagine you are building a house. Quotations are the bricks that have a special decorative pattern— you keep them exactly as they are because they add character. Paraphrases are the standard bricks you shape to fit the walls, showing you can work with the material. Summaries are the foundation, giving the overall shape and stability. Using only one type would make the house either too repetitive, too vague, or too shallow.

> **Remember:** Use quotations for striking language, paraphrases for clear restatement of ideas, and summaries for concise overviews.  

When you combine them wisely, your writing will have a strong voice (your own ideas) supported by solid evidence (the other authors). This balance helps readers trust your argument and understand the topic from multiple angles.

sections.heading: How to Quote Correctly
sections.body:
When you want to use someone else’s exact words in your essay, you are **quoting**. A quote is a tiny piece of another writer’s text that you copy word‑for‑word and place inside quotation marks (“ ”).  

> **Definition:** A *quote* is a verbatim (exact) reproduction of another author’s words, enclosed in quotation marks.

Why quote at all? Because a quote can give your argument authority, show that you have read the source, and let the reader see the original wording that supports your point. Think of a quote like a short, trusted testimonial you might put on a product’s advertisement: the original speaker’s voice adds credibility that your own words alone might not have.

### Step 1 – Choose a short, relevant fragment  
Only include the part of the source that directly backs up your claim. If the original sentence is long, cut it down to the essential words. A good rule of thumb is: **no more than 40 words** for a standard paragraph; longer passages need a block quote (which we will cover later).  

> **Note:** Keeping quotes short helps your own voice stay dominant and prevents the essay from turning into a collage of other people’s sentences.

### Step 2 – Introduce the quote  
Never drop a quote abruptly. Lead into it with a signal phrase that tells the reader who is speaking and why the quote matters. Common signal verbs include *argues, claims, writes, observes,* and *states*.  

Example:  
*Smith (2020) argues that “students learn best when they can see the real‑world relevance of the material” (p. 45).*

In this sentence, **Smith** is the author, **2020** is the year of publication, and **(p. 45)** tells the reader where to find the exact words in the source. The signal phrase (“Smith argues that”) prepares the reader for the quoted material.

### Step 3 – Use quotation marks correctly  
Place double quotation marks at the very beginning and end of the quoted words. If you need to add a word for clarity, put it inside square brackets **[ ]** inside the quotation marks.  

Example:  
*The report states that “the [program] increased attendance by 15 %” (Doe, 2019, p. 12).*

Here, **[program]** clarifies what “it” refers to, without changing the original wording.

### Step 4 – Cite the source immediately  
After the closing quotation mark, include an in‑text citation that matches the style you are using (APA, MLA, Chicago, etc.). The citation usually contains the author’s last name, the year, and the page number. This lets readers locate the original passage and avoids plagiarism.  

> **Remember:** Every quote must have a citation right after it; otherwise the quote looks like your own words.

### Step 5 – Explain the quote  
A quote never stands alone. After you present it, add a sentence (or two) that explains how the quoted words support your argument. This is where your own voice re‑enters.  

Example:  
*Smith’s claim highlights the importance of relevance, which explains why our curriculum redesign focuses on project‑based learning.*

### Putting it all together  
Here is a complete example that follows every step:  

*According to Johnson (2018), “students who write reflective journals show a 20 % improvement in critical‑thinking scores” (p. 78). This statistic demonstrates that reflective writing is not just a feel‑good activity; it has measurable academic benefits, which is why we will incorporate weekly journals into the course.*

### Common pitfalls to avoid  

> **Common mistake:** Using a quote that is too long or only loosely related to your point. Long quotes can drown out your analysis and may be flagged by teachers as “over‑reliance on sources.”

> **In daily life:** Think of a quote like a short excerpt from a movie you share with a friend to prove a point. You wouldn’t recite the whole movie; you pick the exact line that matters.

### Quick checklist for quoting correctly  

1. **Select** a brief, relevant fragment (≤ 40 words).  
2. **Introduce** it with a signal phrase and the author’s name.  
3. **Enclose** the exact words in double quotation marks.  
4. **Add** any clarifying words in square brackets, not altering the original meaning.  
5. **Cite** the source immediately after the quote (author, year, page).  
6. **Explain** why the quote matters for your argument.  

By following these steps, you keep the balance between your own analysis and the evidence you borrow, making your academic writing clear, credible, and persuasive.

sections.heading: Paraphrasing: Putting Ideas into Your Own Words
sections.body:
Paraphrasing means taking someone else’s idea and writing it again **in your own words**. It is not the same as copying, and it is not the same as just changing a few words. When you paraphrase well, you keep the original meaning but express it with a fresh sentence structure and vocabulary that fits the style of your own essay.

> **Definition:** Paraphrasing is the skill of restating a source’s main point using different wording and sentence patterns, while still giving credit to the original author.

Why is this useful? First, it shows that you understand the material. If you can explain a concept without looking at the exact wording, you have processed it. Second, it helps you blend evidence smoothly into your own argument, so the paper sounds like *your* voice rather than a patchwork of quotations.

### Step‑by‑step process

1. **Read the passage slowly**  
   Read the original sentence or short paragraph at least twice. Try to picture the idea in your mind, as if you were explaining it to a friend.

2. **Identify the core idea**  
   Ask yourself: *What is the author really saying here?*  
   Write down a one‑sentence summary in plain language. This is your “note” of the main point, not the exact words.

3. **Highlight any key terms**  
   Some words are essential because they carry specific meaning (e.g., “photosynthesis,” “market equilibrium”). Keep those terms, but you can replace surrounding words.

4. **Switch the sentence structure**  
   Change the order of information. If the original starts with a cause and ends with an effect, try beginning with the effect and then give the cause. Use different grammatical forms (e.g., turn a passive voice into an active voice).

5. **Replace synonyms carefully**  
   Use a thesaurus, but only for words that are not technical. For example, “increase” can become “rise,” but “inflation” should stay “inflation” because the meaning is precise.

6. **Write your version**  
   Combine the steps above into a new sentence. Make sure it still conveys the same meaning as the original.

7. **Compare with the source**  
   Check that you have not accidentally kept a phrase that is too close to the original. If any part looks identical, re‑word it again.

8. **Cite the source**  
   Even though you have rewritten the words, the idea belongs to the original author. Add an in‑text citation in the format required by your style guide (e.g., (Smith 2022)).

### Example

Original:  
*“The rapid expansion of urban areas has led to a significant increase in surface runoff, which in turn raises the risk of flooding during heavy rainstorms.”*

1. Main idea: Urban growth causes more runoff, which makes flooding more likely.  
2. Key terms: “urban areas,” “surface runoff,” “flooding.”  
3. Paraphrase: *Because cities are spreading quickly, more water runs off the ground, so heavy rains are more likely to cause floods (Smith 2022).*

Notice how the cause‑effect relationship is kept, but the wording and order are different.

> **In daily life:** Think of paraphrasing like retelling a movie plot to a friend. You don’t repeat the exact lines from the film; you describe the story in your own voice while still giving credit to the director when you mention the original idea.

### Tips to avoid common pitfalls

- **Don’t just swap a word for a synonym.** Changing “big” to “large” while keeping the rest of the sentence identical is still too close to the source.  
- **Watch out for “copy‑and‑paste” chunks.** Even a phrase of three or four words can be considered plagiarism if it is distinctive.  
- **Keep the meaning exact.** A synonym that slightly changes the nuance (e.g., “help” vs. “assist”) may alter the author’s intent. If you are unsure, keep the original term.

> **Common mistake:** Re‑ordering the words but leaving the same phrasing. This often results in a “patchwork” paraphrase that still looks like the original and can be flagged for plagiarism.

### Quick checklist before you submit

- Have I captured the **main idea** in my own words?  
- Did I **change the sentence structure** and **use different phrasing**?  
- Are all **technical terms** retained where necessary?  
- Did I **add a proper citation** for the idea?  

> **Remember:** Paraphrasing is a tool for showing understanding. If you can explain the concept to a classmate without looking at the text, you have successfully paraphrased it.

sections.heading: Summarising: Condensing Longer Texts
sections.body:
Summarising means taking a longer piece of writing—such as an article, a chapter, or a report—and turning it into a short paragraph that tells the reader only the most important ideas.  

> **Definition:** A summary is a brief restatement of the main points of a source, using your own words and leaving out details, examples, and minor arguments.

Why do we need to summarise?  When you write an essay, you cannot copy whole sections of other authors; the reader would be overwhelmed and you would run out of space for your own analysis.  A good summary lets you show that you understand the source, and it gives your audience the background they need without getting bogged down in unnecessary information.

Think of a movie trailer.  The trailer does not show every scene; it picks the key moments that explain the plot, the main characters, and the tone.  In the same way, a summary selects the “key scenes” of a text—its central claim, the strongest evidence, and the conclusion—while leaving out the side plots.

### Step‑by‑step process

1. **Read the whole text carefully.**  
   Do not try to summarise until you have a clear picture of what the author is arguing.  If the text is long, read it in sections and note the purpose of each paragraph.

2. **Identify the thesis or main argument.**  
   The thesis is the sentence (or a few sentences) that tells you what the author wants you to believe or what problem they are trying to solve.  Write it down in your notebook in plain language.

3. **Find the supporting points.**  
   Look for the major reasons, data, or examples that the author uses to back up the thesis.  Usually there are three to five of these in a typical academic article.

4. **Ignore the details.**  
   Specific statistics, anecdotes, or quotations are useful for a full analysis, but they are not needed in a short summary.  You can safely leave them out unless they are the core of the argument.

5. **Rewrite in your own words.**  
   Using the notes from steps 2 and 3, craft a paragraph that states the thesis first, then lists the main supporting points in the order they appear.  Keep the language simple and avoid copying phrases directly from the source.

6. **Check length.**  
   A good rule of thumb is that a summary should be about **10 %** of the original length.  For a 2,000‑word article, aim for roughly 200 words.

7. **Compare with the original.**  
   After writing, glance back at the source to make sure you have not missed any crucial idea and that you have not added your own opinion.

> **Note:** A summary is *neutral*; it does not include your evaluation, agreement, or disagreement with the source.  Those belong in the analysis part of your essay.

### Example

Original passage (120 words):

> “Climate change is accelerating because of increased greenhouse‑gas emissions from human activities such as burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and industrial processes.  Recent data show that atmospheric carbon dioxide levels have risen from 280 ppm in pre‑industrial times to over 415 ppm today, a rise of nearly 50 %.  This increase has led to higher average global temperatures, more frequent heatwaves, and melting polar ice caps, all of which threaten biodiversity and human livelihoods.”

Summary (≈45 words):

> The author argues that human‑driven greenhouse‑gas emissions are causing rapid climate change.  Carbon dioxide has risen from 280 ppm to over 415 ppm, leading to higher temperatures, more heatwaves, and melting ice, which endanger ecosystems and people.

Notice how the summary captures the main claim (human emissions cause climate change) and the three key pieces of evidence (CO₂ rise, temperature increase, impacts), while omitting the specific percentages and detailed examples.

> **In daily life:** Summarising is like writing a quick text message to a friend about a news article you read—you tell them the headline and the main point, not every quote from the reporter.

### Common pitfalls

> **Common mistake:** Copying whole sentences from the source.  Even if you change a few words, this is still plagiarism.  Always rewrite the idea in your own voice.

> **Remember:** After you have summarised, you can still use a short quotation for a particularly striking phrase, but the quotation must be clearly marked with quotation marks and a citation.

### Quick checklist for a solid summary

- Have you read the whole source first?  
- Does your paragraph start with the author’s main argument?  
- Are the supporting points listed in logical order?  
- Have you removed examples, statistics, and minor details?  
- Is the language completely yours, with no copied phrases?  
- Is the length roughly 10 % of the original?  

If you can answer “yes” to all of these questions, your summary is ready to be inserted into your essay.  It will give readers the essential background they need, while leaving plenty of space for you to add your own analysis and voice.

sections.heading: Balancing Evidence and Your Own Voice
sections.body:
When you write an essay, the goal is to show that you understand the topic **and** that you can think for yourself. Evidence – quotes, paraphrases, and summaries – is the proof that supports your ideas, but it must not drown out your own voice. Think of your essay as a conversation: you are the host, and the evidence are the guests you invite to help explain your point. If the guests talk all the time, the host never gets a chance to speak.

> **Note:** *Balancing evidence and your own voice* means using just enough evidence to support your claim while keeping the majority of the text in your own words.

### Why a balance matters  

1. **Shows critical thinking** – When you explain a quote in your own words, you demonstrate that you have understood it, not just copied it.  
2. **Keeps the reader engaged** – Readers get bored if they have to read long blocks of someone else’s words without hearing your interpretation.  
3. **Avoids plagiarism** – Over‑quoting can look like you are relying on someone else’s work instead of creating your own argument.

### Step‑by‑step strategy  

1. **Set a quote‑length limit**  
   - Decide that no single quotation will be longer than **one sentence** or **15 words** (whichever is shorter).  
   - If a source contains a longer passage that seems essential, **summarise** it instead of quoting it verbatim.  

2. **Mix the three types of evidence**  
   - **Quote**: Use when the original wording is especially powerful, precise, or authoritative.  
   - **Paraphrase**: Restate the idea in a new sentence that fits your own style. This shows you can translate the source’s meaning.  
   - **Summarise**: Condense several sentences or a whole paragraph into a brief statement. Use this when you need background information without getting bogged down in detail.  

   By alternating these three, you create a rhythm: quote → explain → paraphrase → expand → summary → your own analysis.

3. **Add a “bridge” sentence**  
   After any piece of evidence, write a sentence that links it back to your main argument. This is where your voice shines the brightest. For example:  

   > “This statistic shows that …, which supports my claim that …”

4. **Use a “evidence‑to‑comment” ratio**  
   A simple rule of thumb is **2:1** – for every two lines of evidence, write at least one line of your own comment. If you notice you have more evidence than commentary, go back and add more of your own analysis.

5. **Check the flow**  
   Read your paragraph aloud. If you hear more of the source than your own words, trim the quote or replace it with a paraphrase.  

### Everyday comparison  

Imagine you are baking a cake. The flour, sugar, and eggs are the **evidence** – they give the cake its structure and flavor. Your own mixing, timing, and decoration are your **voice**. If you pour in too much flour (over‑quoting), the cake becomes dense and hard to eat. If you add just a pinch of each ingredient and then spend time frosting and arranging the cake, the result is balanced and enjoyable.

> **In daily life:** *Balancing evidence and your own voice is like seasoning a dish – a little salt (quote) enhances the flavor, but too much overwhelms the taste.*

### Common pitfalls to avoid  

- **Copy‑and‑paste syndrome** – dropping a long quote without any explanation.  
- **Paraphrase‑only trap** – never using any direct quotes, which can make your work seem unsupported.  
- **Summary‑only approach** – condensing everything, losing the nuance that a well‑chosen quote provides.

> **Common mistake:** *Leaving a quote without a follow‑up sentence that tells the reader why it matters.*

### Quick checklist  

- [ ] Is each quote ≤ 15 words or one sentence?  
- [ ] Have I mixed quotes, paraphrases, and summaries?  
- [ ] Does every piece of evidence have a bridge sentence that links it to my argument?  
- [ ] Does the paragraph have at least as many of my own sentences as evidence sentences?  
- [ ] Have I read the paragraph aloud to hear the balance?

> **Remember:** *Your essay is your conversation. Let your voice do most of the talking, and let evidence chime in at the right moments.*

sections.heading: Practice Activity: Integrating Evidence
sections.body:
Imagine you have a short article in front of you – maybe a news story about a new park opening in your town. Your task is to turn that article into a short paragraph for an essay, using three different ways to bring the information into your own writing: **quoting**, **paraphrasing**, and **summarising**.  

First, read the article once all the way through. Highlight any sentence that sounds especially powerful or that contains a specific fact you will need to prove later. Those are the spots where a **quote** might work best.  

Next, look for ideas that are important but are expressed in long, complicated sentences. Rewrite those ideas in your own words – that is **paraphrasing**.  

Finally, find sections that give background or describe a series of events. Turn those whole sections into a brief overview – that is **summarising**.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow while you work on the article.

1. **Choose a quote**  
   * Find a sentence that is short, clear, and directly supports the point you want to make.  
   * Copy it exactly as it appears, including punctuation, and put it inside quotation marks.  
   * Add a citation (author, year, page or paragraph number) right after the quote.  

2. **Paraphrase a paragraph**  
   * Read the original paragraph, then look away and write the main idea in your own words.  
   * Keep the meaning the same, but change the wording and sentence structure.  
   * Do **not** copy any phrase longer than three words unless you use quotation marks.  

3. **Summarise a section**  
   * Identify the overall purpose of a longer part of the article (e.g., a description of the park’s design process).  
   * Write one or two sentences that capture the essential points, leaving out details, examples, and opinions.  
   * Cite the whole section, because the summary still relies on the original source.  

> **Definition:** *Quote* – the exact words from a source, enclosed in quotation marks and followed by a citation.  

> **Note:** *Paraphrase* means to restate the original idea in your own language, while keeping the same meaning.  

> **In daily life:** Think of quoting like copying a friend's exact words when you repeat a joke, paraphrasing like retelling the joke in your own style, and summarising like giving the punchline without the whole story.  

> **Remember:** Every piece of evidence you use must be linked to a clear reason why it supports your argument.  

### Checklist for your draft  

| Step | What to look for | Yes / No |
|------|------------------|----------|
| Quote | Exact words, quotation marks, citation, relevant to your claim | |
| Paraphrase | Same meaning, different wording, no long phrases copied, citation | |
| Summarise | Main idea only, concise (1‑2 sentences), citation for whole section | |
| Integration | Quote, paraphrase, and summary flow together; your own voice appears between them | |
| Attribution | Every piece of evidence has a citation in the correct format | |

### How to use the checklist  

1. **Read your paragraph aloud.** Does it sound like a single, smooth piece of writing, or does it feel choppy? If it feels choppy, you may have over‑quoted or not added enough of your own explanation.  

2. **Mark each piece of evidence** with a coloured pen: green for quotes, blue for paraphrases, orange for summaries. Then check the corresponding row in the table.  

3. **Ask yourself:** “Did I explain why this evidence matters?” If the answer is no, add a short sentence after the evidence that links it to your argument.  

4. **Double‑check citations.** Make sure the author’s name, year, and page/paragraph number are present and formatted consistently.  

### Example (short excerpt)  

Original article sentence:  
> “The new Riverside Park will feature a 2‑kilometre walking trail, native‑plant gardens, and a solar‑powered playground.”  

Your paragraph might look like this:  

> The city’s latest project, Riverside Park, promises several eco‑friendly amenities. As the council announced, “The new Riverside Park will feature a 2‑kilometre walking trail, native‑plant gardens, and a solar‑powered playground” (City Council, 2024, para. 4). In other words, the park will include a long trail for walkers, gardens that use local plants, and a playground that runs on solar energy. Overall, the development aims to combine recreation with sustainability (City Council, 2024).  

Notice how the quote gives the exact wording, the paraphrase rewrites it, and the summary at the end ties the whole idea back to the essay’s focus on sustainable urban design.  

Now you are ready to try it yourself. Choose a short article (about 300‑400 words), apply the three techniques, and run your work through the checklist. When each row says **Yes**, you have successfully integrated evidence while keeping your own voice clear and strong. Good luck!

sections.heading: Reflection and Checklist
sections.body:
When you finish a draft, it is easy to feel that the work is complete because the ideas are all on the page.  
But a good academic essay does more than just present facts – it shows that you have **chosen** the right evidence, **explained** it in your own voice, and **balanced** it so the reader can see how the evidence supports your argument.  

Think of your essay like a sandwich. The bread slices are your own ideas; the fillings are the pieces of evidence you add. If you pile on too much filling, the sandwich becomes messy and hard to bite. If you use only a tiny bit of filling, the sandwich feels dry and unsatisfying. The reflection checklist below helps you taste the sandwich before you serve it to your teacher.

> **Remember:** A checklist is a short list of questions you ask yourself. It works like a quick self‑test that catches common problems before you submit your work.

### Self‑assessment checklist for using evidence

| ✔️ Question | Why it matters |
|------------|----------------|
| **1. Have I used at least three different types of evidence (facts, statistics, expert opinion, examples, or anecdotes)?** | Using a mix shows you can draw from many sources and makes your argument stronger. |
| **2. Does each quotation include a proper citation and fit naturally into my sentence?** | Proper citations give credit and avoid plagiarism; smooth integration keeps the flow. |
| **3. For every quotation, have I added a comment that explains *why* it matters to my point?** | The comment is the “bread” that holds the evidence together; without it the reader does not know its purpose. |
| **4. Have I paraphrased or summarized at least as much as I have quoted?** | Paraphrasing shows you understand the source and keeps your own voice dominant. |
| **5. Is the total length of quotations less than 30 % of the whole essay?** | Over‑quoting can drown out your own analysis; the 30 % rule is a common guideline. |
| **6. Did I check that every source is listed correctly in the bibliography?** | A complete bibliography proves you have done the research and lets readers find the original material. |
| **7. Have I read the essay aloud to hear whether the evidence feels balanced?** | Reading aloud reveals awkward jumps between your voice and the sources. |
| **8. Did I remove any “filler” quotes that repeat the same idea?** | Repeating evidence wastes space and can confuse the reader. |

### How to use the checklist

1. **Print or copy the table** onto a separate sheet of paper.  
2. **Read each question** carefully after you finish a draft.  
3. **Mark “yes” or “no”** for each item. If you answer “no,” go back to the relevant paragraph and fix it.  
4. **Count the “yes” answers.** If you have at least 7‑8 “yes” responses, your evidence handling is likely solid.  

> **In daily life:** Think of the checklist like a grocery list before you shop. You look at the list, see what you already have, and add only the missing items. The same idea works for evidence: you see what you already have and add only what is needed.

### Spotting over‑quoting

A quick visual cue can help: highlight every block of quoted text in a bright colour. Then, using a ruler or the cursor, count how many lines of your essay are highlighted. If the highlighted portion stretches across more than one‑third of the total lines, you probably have too many quotes.

You can also use a simple equation to estimate the balance:

$$
\text{Quote Ratio} = \frac{\text{Number of quoted words}}{\text{Total word count}}
$$

If the Quote Ratio is greater than $0.30$, rewrite some quotes as paraphrases or summaries.

### Final reflection

Before you click “submit,” take a minute to ask yourself:

- **Did I let my own ideas shine through?**  
- **Did every piece of evidence have a clear purpose?**  
- **Is the essay readable without constantly stopping to check the bibliography?**  

If the answer to any of these is “no,” use the checklist to guide a quick revision. By treating your draft as a sandwich that you can taste and adjust, you ensure that the final product is both flavorful and well‑balanced.

practice.q: What is the main reason for using different types of evidence (e.g., statistics, expert testimony, examples) in an academic essay?
practice.a: Using different types of evidence strengthens an argument because each kind supports the claim in a unique way. Statistics provide numerical proof, expert testimony adds authority, and examples illustrate the idea in a concrete context. Together they make the argument more convincing and show the writer has considered multiple perspectives.

practice.q: When you paraphrase a sentence, what must you still include to avoid plagiarism?
practice.a: Even after paraphrasing, you must include an in‑text citation that gives credit to the original author and source. This shows you are using someone else’s ideas, even though the wording is yours.

practice.q: Compare quoting directly with paraphrasing. When is each method more appropriate in an essay?
practice.a: Quoting directly is best when the original wording is especially clear, powerful, or authoritative, or when you need to discuss the exact phrasing. Paraphrasing is better when you want to simplify complex language, integrate the idea smoothly into your own style, or when the exact words are not crucial. Use quotes sparingly to support key points; use paraphrase for most of the evidence to keep your voice dominant.

practice.q: You have a paragraph that currently contains a long quotation of 40 words. Rewrite the paragraph by summarising the main point of the quotation in two sentences and add an appropriate citation.
practice.a: First, read the quotation and identify its core idea. Suppose the quote says: “Recent studies show that 78 % of high school students who engage in daily reading improve their vocabulary scores by at least 15 % over a semester.” Summarise: Recent research indicates that most high‑school students who read daily see a significant boost in vocabulary. In fact, scores can rise by around fifteen percent in just one semester (Smith, 2023). This summary captures the essential information, shortens the text, and still gives credit.

practice.q: Explain how you would balance evidence and your own voice in a 1500‑word research essay. Include at least three specific strategies.
practice.a: 1. **Use evidence to support, not replace, your argument** – after presenting a piece of evidence, follow it with analysis that explains how it relates to your thesis. 2. **Limit direct quotes** – keep quotes under 10 % of the total word count; instead, paraphrase most sources, which forces you to reinterpret the ideas in your own words. 3. **Create a clear structure** – start each paragraph with a topic sentence (your voice), insert evidence, then end with a concluding sentence that ties the evidence back to your main claim. This pattern ensures your voice remains the thread that connects all evidence.

practice.q: You are writing a literature review and need to integrate three sources: a statistical report, an expert’s opinion, and a case study. Draft a short paragraph (about 120 words) that weaves these three types of evidence together, includes proper citations, and maintains your analytical voice.
practice.a:
Begin with your own claim, then embed each evidence type:
Recent data suggest that 62 % of teenagers experience anxiety during exam periods (National Health Survey, 2022). This trend is echoed by Dr. Lee, a child‑psychology specialist, who argues that high‑stakes testing amplifies stress hormones in adolescents (Lee, 2023). Supporting both points, a case study from Riverside High showed that implementing mindfulness breaks reduced anxiety scores by 20 % over a semester (Riverside School Board, 2024). Together, these findings indicate that academic pressure is a measurable risk factor, but targeted interventions can mitigate its impact. The paragraph starts with your analysis, inserts the three evidence types with citations, and ends by linking them back to your overarching argument.

data.recap: The lesson explains why writers use three types of evidence—quoting, paraphrasing, and summarising—to support their arguments. It shows how each method works, when to choose it, and how to keep the writer’s own voice dominant. Practical steps and a checklist help students apply these techniques correctly.

lessons.title: Citing Sources
lessons.focus: Referencing styles, in-text citations and building a reference list

data.title: Citing Sources
data.summary: In this lesson students learn how to correctly cite sources using different referencing styles, create in‑text citations, and compile a reference list. Mastering these skills ensures their writing is credible and avoids plagiarism.
objectives: Identify the main features of common referencing styles (APA, MLA, Harvard).
Create correct in‑text citations for quotes, paraphrases, and summaries.
Assemble a properly formatted reference list for a range of source types.
Apply consistent citation practice throughout an essay.
data.prerequisites: Students should already know how to use evidence in an essay and understand the basics of academic writing.
why: Accurate citations show where information comes from, giving readers a way to verify facts and follow up on research. This builds trust and demonstrates academic honesty.
In the workplace and higher education, proper referencing is required for reports, proposals, and publications. Failing to cite correctly can lead to loss of credibility or even legal issues.

sections.heading: Why Referencing Matters
sections.body:
When you write an essay, a report, or any piece of academic work, you are building on ideas that already exist.  
A **citation** is a short note that tells the reader exactly where you found each idea, fact, or quotation.  

> **Definition:** *Citation* – a brief reference in the text that points to a full description of the source in your reference list.  

Why do we need these little notes?  

1. **Give credit where it is due** – Imagine a friend shows you a cool trick in a video game and you later describe the trick to another friend without saying where you learned it. Your first friend would feel ignored, right? In the same way, scholars deserve recognition for the work they have done. By citing, you acknowledge their contribution.  

2. **Show that your work is trustworthy** – Readers can check the original source to see if you have reported it correctly. If you claim that “the Earth’s average temperature rose by 1.2 °C in the last decade” without a citation, a skeptical reader has no way to verify that number. Providing a source lets the reader see the evidence for themselves, which makes your argument stronger.  

3. **Avoid plagiarism** – *Plagiarism* is the act of using someone else’s words or ideas and presenting them as your own. It is considered dishonest because it hides the true origin of the information. Academic institutions treat plagiarism as a serious breach of **academic integrity**, which is the principle of being honest and responsible in learning.  

> **Note:** *Academic integrity* – the commitment to honesty, fairness, and responsibility in scholarly work.  

4. **Help others find more information** – A good citation works like a road sign. If a reader is interested in learning more about a topic, the citation points them to the exact book, article, or website where they can continue their research.  

### Everyday comparison  

Think of a recipe you found online. If you bake a cake using that recipe and then tell your friends “I made this amazing cake,” you would normally mention where you got the recipe. That way, your friends can look up the original page if they want to try it themselves. The citation in an academic paper works the same way: it tells the reader, “Here is the source of this idea; you can read more if you wish.”  

### Consequences of not citing  

- **Loss of marks** – Teachers and examiners often deduct points for missing citations because they cannot be sure the work is original.  
- **Academic penalties** – In many schools and universities, plagiarism can lead to a failing grade, a formal warning, or even expulsion.  
- **Damaged reputation** – If a published paper is found to have uncited material, the author’s credibility suffers, and future publishers may be reluctant to accept their work.  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to add a citation for a paraphrased idea (re‑wording someone’s point in your own words). Even if you change the wording, the idea still belongs to the original author and must be cited.  

### Linking citations to integrity  

Academic integrity is not just a rule; it is the foundation of trustworthy knowledge. When everyone cites properly, the whole community can trust that the information shared is reliable and that each contributor receives fair recognition. This creates a cycle: proper citation → trust → more collaboration → better learning.  

> **Remember:** Citing is a simple act that protects you, respects others, and keeps the flow of knowledge honest and clear.  

In summary, citations are the glue that holds academic work together. They give credit, allow verification, prevent plagiarism, and guide readers to further information. Skipping them harms your grade, your reputation, and the whole scholarly conversation. By understanding why referencing matters, you are already taking the first step toward becoming a responsible and effective writer.

sections.heading: Overview of Common Referencing Styles
sections.body:
When you write an essay, a report, or a research paper you are not working alone.  
You are building on ideas that other people have already created.  
A *referencing style* is simply a set of rules that tells you how to show where those ideas came from.  
Using a consistent style lets readers find the original source quickly, and it shows that you respect other people's work.

### The three most common styles

| Style | When you usually see it | How it shows the source in the text |
|-------|------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **APA** (American Psychological Association) | Social sciences, psychology, education | **author‑date**: (Smith, 2020) |
| **MLA** (Modern Language Association) | Humanities, literature, arts | **author‑page**: (Smith 45) |
| **Harvard** | Many universities, especially in the UK and Australia | **author‑date** (very similar to APA) |

All three styles require two things:

1. **In‑text citation** – a short note inside your paragraph that points to the full reference.  
2. **Reference list** – a complete list of all sources at the end of your work.

The main visual difference is *what comes after the author’s name*.

> **Definition:** *author‑date* means you write the author’s last name followed by the year of publication, e.g., (Brown 2018).  
> **Definition:** *author‑page* means you write the author’s last name followed by the page number where the information appears, e.g., (Brown 23).

### Why the two formats exist

Think of a library.  
If you ask the librarian for a book, you might give the **title** (like an author‑date citation) or you might give the **shelf number** (like an author‑page citation).  
Both point to the same book, but the shelf number tells the librarian exactly where to find the specific page you need.  

In the **author‑date** system, the year tells the reader which version of a work you used. This is useful when a source has many editions or when research moves quickly, as in the sciences.  

In the **author‑page** system, the page number tells the reader exactly where the quoted or paraphrased idea appears. This is helpful in literature or history, where the exact wording on a page matters.

### Quick visual comparison

- **APA**:  
  In‑text: $$Citation = (Author, Year)$$  
  Reference list entry: Author, A. A. (Year). *Title of the work*. Publisher.

- **MLA**:  
  In‑text: $$Citation = (Author Page)$$  
  Works‑Cited entry: Author, Firstname. *Title of the Work*. Publisher, Year.

- **Harvard**:  
  In‑text: $$Citation = (Author, Year)$$  
  Reference list entry: Author, A., Year. *Title of the work*. Place of publication: Publisher.

> **Note:** The punctuation around the author, year, and page can differ. APA uses a comma between author and year, while MLA puts a space between author and page number. Harvard usually follows the APA pattern but may vary in the reference list layout.

### How to choose which style to use

1. **Check the assignment guidelines** – teachers almost always tell you which style they expect.  
2. **Look at the subject area** – sciences → APA, humanities → MLA, many UK courses → Harvard.  
3. **Be consistent** – once you pick a style, use it for every citation in that paper. Switching back and forth is a common mistake that confuses readers.

> **Common mistake:** Mixing APA’s author‑date in‑text citations with MLA’s author‑page reference list. Always keep the whole paper in the same style.

### Remember the purpose

The goal of any referencing style is to make the trail from your writing back to the original source as clear as possible.  
If a reader sees (Jones, 2015) they can go to the reference list, find Jones’s 2015 work, and locate the exact page if needed.  
If they see (Jones 78) they know you are pointing to page 78 of Jones’s book, which they can look up directly.

> **Remember:** The style you use does not change the quality of your ideas; it only changes how you show where those ideas came from. A clean, consistent citation format lets your arguments shine without distraction.

sections.heading: In‑Text Citations: Basics
sections.body:
When you write a paper you are talking to a reader who has never heard your ideas before.  
If you use someone else’s words or ideas, you must tell the reader **where** those words came from.  
That short note inside the sentence is called an *in‑text citation*.  

> **Definition:** An *in‑text citation* is a brief reference placed inside the body of your essay that points the reader to the full details of the source in your reference list.  

Why it matters  
- It shows respect for the original author’s work.  
- It lets readers check the source if they want more information.  
- It protects you from accusations of plagiarism (using someone’s work without credit).  

### The three ways you might use a source  

1. **Direct quote** – you copy the exact words, word for word.  
2. **Paraphrase** – you restate the idea in your own words, keeping the meaning the same.  
3. **Summary** – you give a short overview of the main point, leaving out details.  

All three need a citation, but the format changes slightly depending on the referencing style you are using. Below are the three most common styles: **APA (American Psychological Association)**, **MLA (Modern Language Association)**, and **Harvard**.  

---

#### 1. Direct quotes  

**APA** – put the author’s last name, the year, and the page number in parentheses after the quote.  

> “Learning is a lifelong process” (Smith, 2020, p. 15).  

If the author’s name is already part of the sentence, only the year and page go in parentheses.  

> Smith (2020) writes, “Learning is a lifelong process” (p. 15).  

**MLA** – use the author’s last name and the page number, no year.  

> “Learning is a lifelong process” (Smith 15).  

If the author is named in the text, just add the page number.  

> Smith argues that “learning is a lifelong process” (15).  

**Harvard** – similar to APA but the page number follows a comma after the year.  

> “Learning is a lifelong process” (Smith, 2020, p. 15).  

---

#### 2. Paraphrasing  

When you restate the idea, you still give credit, but you do not need a page number unless the source is very specific.  

**APA** – author and year are enough.  

> Smith (2020) suggests that learning continues throughout life.  

If the author is not mentioned in the sentence, put both in parentheses.  

> Learning continues throughout life (Smith, 2020).  

**MLA** – author’s name only; page number is optional.  

> Smith argues that learning continues throughout life.  

**Harvard** – author and year, like APA.  

> Smith (2020) argues that learning continues throughout life.  

---

#### 3. Summarizing  

A summary condenses a whole chapter or article. The citation works the same as for a paraphrase.  

**APA**  

> Recent research shows that lifelong learning improves mental health (Jones, 2019).  

**MLA**  

> Recent research shows that lifelong learning improves mental health (Jones 42).  

**Harvard**  

> Recent research shows that lifelong learning improves mental health (Jones, 2019).  

> **In daily life:** Think of an in‑text citation like a quick “thank‑you” note you slip into a conversation. You say, “I read that in a book by Dr. Lee,” and later you give the full book details.  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to add the page number for a direct quote. Remember, a quote is a *verbatim* copy, so the reader must know exactly where to find it.  

> **Remember:** Every time you quote, paraphrase, or summarize, place a citation **immediately after** the borrowed material, before the period that ends the sentence.  

Here is a simple formula you can keep in mind for each style:  

$$ \text{Citation} = \begin{cases}
(\text{Author}, \text{Year}, p.\ \text{Page}) & \text{APA / Harvard (quote)}\\[4pt]
(\text{Author}\ \text{Page}) & \text{MLA (quote)}\\[4pt]
(\text{Author}, \text{Year}) & \text{APA / Harvard (paraphrase/summary)}\\[4pt]
(\text{Author}) & \text{MLA (paraphrase/summary)}
\end{cases} $$  

By following these patterns you will give clear credit, help your reader, and keep your work honest.

sections.heading: In‑Text Citations: Special Cases
sections.body:
When you quote or paraphrase someone’s ideas, you must tell the reader exactly where those ideas came from. This is called an **in‑text citation**. Most of the time the citation is simple: (Smith 2020) or (Smith & Jones, 2020). But sometimes the source does not fit the usual pattern. Below are the special situations you may meet and how to handle each one correctly.

> **Definition:** *In‑text citation* – a brief note inside the sentence that points the reader to the full reference in the reference list.

### 1. More than three authors  
If a work has **two** authors, list both every time: (Brown & Lee, 2019).  
If a work has **three or more** authors, you do **not** write every name after the first mention. Instead use the first author’s surname followed by “et al.”, which is short for the Latin *et alii* meaning “and others”.  

Example:  
- First citation: (Garcia, Patel, & Nguyen, 2021) – you can write all three if you wish.  
- Later citations: (Garcia *et al.*, 2021).  

Why? It keeps the text tidy and avoids long strings of names that distract the reader.

> **In daily life:** Think of a group project where you introduce the team once (“Alice, Bob, and Charlie worked on the experiment”). After that you just say “the team” instead of naming everyone again.

### 2. No author listed  
Sometimes a source, such as a webpage or a report, does not give a personal author. Use the **title** of the work instead. If the title is long, you can shorten it to the first few words, put it in quotation marks, and add the year.

Example:  
- Full title: *Global Climate Change: Impacts and Solutions* (2022).  
- In‑text citation: (“Global Climate Change,” 2022).  

If the source is a **periodical** (like a newspaper) and the title is very short, you can use the **first few words** without quotation marks, but keep the year.

> **Note:** Always keep the same shortened title throughout the paper so the reader can match it to the reference list.

### 3. Corporate author  
When an organization, government agency, or company writes a document, the organization itself is the author. Write the full name of the organization in the citation.

Example:  
- (World Health Organization, 2020)  
- (National Aeronautics and Space Administration, 2018)  

If the corporate name is very long and you will cite it many times, you may introduce an abbreviation the first time:  

> **Definition:** *Abbreviation* – a shortened form of a longer name, introduced once and then used thereafter.  

First citation: (National Aeronautics and Space Administration **[NASA]**, 2018)  
Later citations: (NASA, 2018)  

This mirrors how we often use nicknames for people we know well.

### 4. Secondary citations (citing a source you found inside another source)  
Sometimes you read a useful idea in a book, but the original research is in an older article you do not have. You can still give credit, but you must show both the original author and the source you actually consulted. Write the original author’s name and year, then add “as cited in” followed by the author and year of the source you read.

Example:  
- Original: Miller (1975) argued that…  
- You read it in: Johnson (2020).  

In‑text citation: (Miller, 1975, *as cited in* Johnson, 2020)  

Why is this useful? It tells the reader that the idea originated with Miller, while also being honest that you did not examine Miller’s work directly.

> **Common mistake:** Listing only the secondary source (Johnson, 2020) and pretending you read Miller’s article. This can mislead readers and is considered poor academic practice.

### Putting the rules together  

When you write a sentence with a special case, follow these steps:

1. Identify the type of source (multiple authors, no author, corporate author, secondary).  
2. Choose the correct format (surname et al., title, organization name, or “as cited in”).  
3. Insert the year immediately after the name or title, separated by a comma.  
4. Keep the punctuation consistent: always use parentheses and separate multiple items with commas.

For example:  

> “Recent climate models show faster warming trends (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2023).”  

If the same report has three authors, you would write:  

> “Recent climate models show faster warming trends (IPCC *et al.*, 2023).”

### Quick checklist  

- **Two authors:** list both each time.  
- **Three or more:** first author + *et al.* after first full citation.  
- **No author:** use shortened title in quotes.  
- **Corporate author:** write full organization name; introduce abbreviation if needed.  
- **Secondary citation:** original author *as cited in* secondary source.

> **Remember:** Consistency is key. Once you pick a style for a special case, use it the same way throughout your paper so the reader can easily follow your sources.

sections.heading: Building a Reference List
sections.body:
When you finish an essay, the **reference list** (sometimes called a bibliography) is the place where you give full details of every source you mentioned in the text.  
Think of it like the “ingredients list” on a food package: just as a shopper can see exactly what went into the product, a reader can see exactly what you used to build your argument.  

### 1. General rules for the whole list  

1. **Order** – Arrange the entries alphabetically by the surname (last name) of the first author. If a source has no author, start with the title (ignore the word *The* or *A*).  
2. **Spacing** – Use a hanging indent: the first line of each entry is flush left, and any following lines are indented half an inch. This makes each entry easy to scan.  
3. **Punctuation** – Most styles separate the main parts of a citation with commas, and end the whole entry with a period.  
4. **Font** – Keep the same font and size you used in the essay (usually 12‑point Times New Roman or Arial).  

> **Remember:** Consistency is key. Pick one referencing style (e.g., APA, Harvard, Chicago) and apply its rules to every entry.

### 2. Books  

A typical book entry contains: author(s), year, title (italicised), edition (if not the first), place of publication, and publisher.

```
Smith, J. (2020). *Understanding Climate Change* (2nd ed.). London: Green Earth Press.
```

- **Author(s)** – List surname first, then initials. Use an ampersand (&) before the last author if there are multiple.  
- **Year** – Put the year in parentheses right after the author(s).  
- **Title** – Italicise the whole title; only the first word and proper nouns are capitalised (sentence case).  
- **Edition** – Include only if it is not the first edition; write “2nd ed.”, “3rd ed.”, etc.  
- **Place & Publisher** – Separate the city and the publisher with a colon.

### 3. Journal articles  

Journal articles need the article title, journal title, volume, issue, page range, and DOI (digital object identifier) if available.

```
Lee, A., & Patel, R. (2019). Social media and teenage anxiety. *Journal of Youth Studies*, 15(3), 210‑225. https://doi.org/10.1080/13676261.2019.1601234
```

- **Journal title** – Italicise and use title case (capitalize major words).  
- **Volume** – Italicise the volume number.  
- **Issue** – Put the issue number in parentheses, not italicised.  
- **Pages** – Use an en‑dash (‑) between the first and last page.  
- **DOI** – A permanent link; start with “https://doi.org/”. If no DOI, you may give the URL of the journal’s homepage.

### 4. Websites  

Web sources often lack some of the details required for books or journals, so you include what you have: author (if known), year (or “n.d.” for no date), title of the page, website name, and the full URL. Add the date you accessed the page if the content might change.

```
World Health Organization. (2022). Nutrition and health guidelines. WHO. https://www.who.int/nutrition/guidelines (accessed 10 Oct 2023)
```

- **Author** – If the organization is the author, write its full name.  
- **Year** – Use the year the page was published or updated; if none, write “n.d.” (no date).  
- **Title** – Sentence case, not italicised.  
- **Website name** – Usually the organization or the site’s title; italicise if the style requires it.  
- **URL** – Provide the complete web address; do not add a period after it to avoid confusion.

### 5. Other common sources  

| Source type | Typical elements | Example |
|------------|------------------|---------|
| **Edited book chapter** | Author of chapter, year, chapter title, *In* editor(s) (Eds.), book title, pages, publisher | Brown, L. (2018). Climate policy in Europe. *In* M. Green & S. White (Eds.), *Environmental Law* (pp. 45‑68). New York: Legal Press. |
| **Conference paper** | Author, year, paper title, *In* conference name, location, pages | Kumar, S. (2021). AI in education. *In* Proceedings of the International Conference on Learning Technologies, Berlin, 112‑119. |
| **Report (government or NGO)** | Author/agency, year, title (italicised), report number (if any), publisher, URL | Department for Education. (2020). *Annual school performance report* (Report No. 2020‑05). London: DfE. https://www.education.gov.uk/report2020 |

> **In daily life:** A reference list works like a “contact list” on your phone – it lets anyone quickly find the exact source you used, just as a phone number lets you call a friend.

### 6. Putting it together  

1. Gather all sources you cited.  
2. Write each entry following the pattern for its type.  
3. Sort the list alphabetically.  
4. Apply the hanging indent and check punctuation.  

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting the hanging indent makes the list look like a paragraph, which hides where one source ends and the next begins.  

Finally, give the whole list a clear heading such as **References** or **Bibliography** (depending on the style) and place it on a new page after the main text. This tidy, consistent list shows respect for the original authors and helps your readers trust the quality of your work.

sections.heading: Putting It All Together
sections.body:
Imagine you have written a short paragraph about climate change and you now need to show where the ideas came from.  
Below we will take a plain paragraph, add the correct **in‑text citations**, and then create a **reference list** that matches the citations.  
We will use the **APA 7th** style because it is common in many school subjects, but the same steps work for other styles – you only change the punctuation and order.

---

### 1. The original paragraph (no citations)

> Climate change is causing more extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall.  
> Scientists say that the increase in greenhouse gases from human activities is the main driver of global warming.  
> Reducing carbon emissions can limit future damage, but it requires cooperation from governments, businesses, and individuals.

---

### 2. Identify the sources you used

| Idea in the paragraph | Source you will cite |
|-----------------------|----------------------|
| “more extreme weather events … heatwaves and heavy rainfall” | IPCC, 2021 report |
| “increase in greenhouse gases … main driver of global warming” | NASA, 2022 climate overview |
| “Reducing carbon emissions can limit future damage” | Smith & Lee, 2020 study on mitigation |

> **Remember:** Write down every fact, statistic, or idea that is not your own. This makes it easy to add citations later.

---

### 3. Add in‑text citations

In APA style, an in‑text citation includes the author’s last name(s) and the year of publication, placed in parentheses right after the relevant sentence.

> Climate change is causing more extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall (IPCC, 2021).  
> Scientists say that the increase in greenhouse gases from human activities is the main driver of global warming (NASA, 2022).  
> Reducing carbon emissions can limit future damage, but it requires cooperation from governments, businesses, and individuals (Smith & Lee, 2020).

> **Definition:** *In‑text citation* – a brief reference inside the paragraph that points the reader to the full source in the reference list.

---

### 4. Build the reference list

The reference list appears at the end of the essay on a new page titled **References**.  
Each entry must contain enough information for a reader to locate the source. In APA, the order is: Author(s). (Year). *Title of work*. Publisher or journal, volume(issue), pages. DOI or URL if available.

Here are the three entries that match our citations:

```
References

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. (2021). *Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis*. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/

National Aeronautics and Space Administration. (2022). *Climate change: How do we know?* https://climate.nasa.gov/evidence/

Smith, J., & Lee, R. (2020). Mitigation strategies to limit global warming. *Journal of Environmental Policy*, 15(3), 45‑58. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jep.2020.01.004
```

> **Note:** The reference list is **alphabetical** by the first author’s last name, not by the order you cited them in the text.

---

### 5. Put everything together

Now copy the paragraph with citations, add a blank line, write **References**, and list the three entries exactly as shown. The final excerpt looks like this:

> Climate change is causing more extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall (IPCC, 2021).  
> Scientists say that the increase in greenhouse gases from human activities is the main driver of global warming (NASA, 2022).  
> Reducing carbon emissions can limit future damage, but it requires cooperation from governments, businesses, and individuals (Smith & Lee, 2020).

> References  
> 
> Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. (2021). *Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis*. https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/  
> 
> National Aeronautics and Space Administration. (2022). *Climate change: How do we know?* https://climate.nasa.gov/evidence/  
> 
> Smith, J., & Lee, R. (2020). Mitigation strategies to limit global warming. *Journal of Environmental Policy*, 15(3), 45‑58. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jep.2020.01.004

> **In daily life:** Adding citations is like putting a label on a borrowed book. The label tells others where the book came from, so they can find it again if they want.

---

### 6. Quick checklist before you submit

1. Every claim that is not common knowledge has a citation.  
2. All citations in the text appear **once** in the reference list.  
3. The reference list is alphabetised and uses the correct punctuation for the chosen style.  
4. Font, spacing, and indentation follow the style guide (APA uses a hanging indent of 0.5 in).  

Follow these steps for any short essay, and you will turn a plain paragraph into a properly referenced piece of academic writing.

sections.heading: Checking Your Work
sections.body:
When you finish writing a paper, the last thing you should do is **check** it.  
Checking is like proofreading a road map before you hand it to a driver – you want to be sure every street name is spelled correctly, the symbols are clear, and there are no missing turns that could cause a crash. In academic writing, the “roads” are your citations and reference list. A careful check makes sure the reader can follow your trail of evidence without getting lost.

### Step‑by‑step checklist

1. **Match every in‑text citation to a reference entry**  
   - Scan the text from the beginning to the end. Each time you see a citation (e.g., (Smith 2020) or [1]), write down the author’s name or number.  
   - Then go to the reference list and verify that the same author and year (or number) appear there.  
   - If you find a citation that has no matching entry, add it. If an entry has no citation in the text, delete it.

2. **Check the order and format of the reference list**  
   - Different styles have different rules. For example, APA orders references alphabetically by the first author’s last name, while Vancouver orders them numerically in the order they appear in the text.  
   - Make sure the list follows the rule for the style you are using.  
   - Look at each entry: are the author names, year, title, journal, volume, issue, and page numbers all present and in the right places?  

3. **Verify punctuation and spacing**  
   - Small marks such as commas, periods, and brackets can change the meaning of a citation.  
   - In APA, a typical journal article looks like:  
   $$\text{Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of article. *Journal Name*, 12(3), 45–67.}$$  
   - Notice the period after the year, the italicised journal name, the comma after the volume number, and the en‑dash between page numbers.  
   - Compare each entry to a reliable example from your style guide and correct any differences.

4. **Watch out for common typographical errors**  
   - Misspelling an author’s name or a journal title can make it impossible for a reader to locate the source.  
   - Double‑check capitalisation: only the first word of a article title and proper nouns are capitalised in APA, while all major words are capitalised in MLA.  

5. **Confirm consistency of abbreviations and abbreviations**  
   - If you abbreviate a journal name (e.g., *J. Biol. Chem.*), use the same abbreviation everywhere.  
   - Do not mix full names and abbreviations in the same list.  

6. **Check that you have used the correct citation style throughout**  
   - It is easy to start with one style and slip into another, especially if you copy a reference from a source that uses a different format.  
   - Look at the first ten entries; if they all follow the same pattern, the rest likely do too.  

7. **Run a final spell‑check and grammar check**  
   - Most word processors have built‑in tools. They will not catch every citation error, but they will catch stray commas, missing periods, and other simple mistakes.  

> **Note:** A consistent reference list is not just about looking tidy; it shows that you respect the work of other scholars and helps readers verify your claims.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to update the reference list after adding or deleting a citation in the text. This creates “orphan” entries that confuse readers and may be marked as plagiarism.

> **Remember:** Treat your reference list like a grocery receipt – every item you mention in the text must appear on the list, and every item on the list must have been bought (cited) in the text.

### Quick self‑test

- **All citations present?** Tick each citation and match it to the list.  
- **All entries used?** Cross‑out any reference that has no citation.  
- **Style correct?** Compare a sample entry to the official style guide.  
- **Punctuation right?** Look for missing commas, periods, or italics.  
- **Spelling checked?** Verify author names and journal titles.

If you can answer “yes” to every question, your paper’s citations are ready for submission. Just like a driver checks the mirrors before leaving the garage, a writer checks the citations before handing in the work. This final step protects your credibility and makes your research easy for others to follow.

practice.q: What is the main purpose of including an in‑text citation in an academic paragraph?
practice.a: The main purpose is to show where the information comes from, giving credit to the original author and allowing readers to find the source. This avoids plagiarism and strengthens the writer’s argument by showing evidence.

practice.q: In the Harvard style, how would you cite a book by Jane Smith published in 2020 with the title *Learning Science* in the text?
practice.a: In Harvard style, you place the author's surname, year, and (if needed) page number in parentheses after the information. Example: (Smith, 2020). If you quote a specific page, add the page: (Smith, 2020, p. 45).

practice.q: Compare how a journal article is referenced in the reference list using APA 7th edition and MLA 9th edition. List the main differences in order of elements.
practice.a:
APA 7th: Author(s). (Year). Title of article. *Title of Journal*, volume number(issue number), page range. DOI (if available).
MLA 9th: Author(s). "Title of Article." *Title of Journal*, vol. number, no. issue number, Year, pp. page range. DOI or URL (if online).
Key differences: APA puts the year immediately after the author and uses sentence case for the article title; MLA places the year later and uses title case for the article title. APA uses italics for the journal name and volume, while MLA also italicises the journal but adds “vol.” and “no.” before numbers. APA includes DOI after a period; MLA adds DOI/URL at the end.

practice.q: Apply the Chicago author‑date style to create an in‑text citation for a source with two authors, Alex Rivera and Priya Patel, published in 2018, when you are quoting page 112.
practice.a: In Chicago author‑date, list both surnames, the year, and the page number in parentheses: (Rivera and Patel 2018, 112). This appears directly after the quoted material.

practice.q: You have used three sources in a paragraph: a book (Brown 2015), a journal article (Lee 2019), and a website with no author (World Health Org. 2022). Show how you would combine these into a single in‑text citation using APA 7th edition, and then write the corresponding reference list entries for each source.
practice.a:
Combined in‑text citation in APA 7th: (Brown, 2015; Lee, 2019; World Health Organization, 2022).
Reference list entries:
Brown, J. (2015). *Understanding Climate Change*. Green Press.
Lee, S. (2019). Impacts of urbanization on river ecosystems. *Environmental Research*, 45(3), 210‑225. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envres.2019.01.012
World Health Organization. (2022, March 10). Global health statistics 2022. https://www.who.int/data/health-statistics-2022

practice.q: Explain why it is important to adapt your reference list to the specific style required by a journal, and describe two potential consequences of submitting a manuscript with incorrectly formatted references.
practice.a: Adapting the reference list shows that the author follows the journal’s editorial standards, making the paper look professional and ensuring that reviewers and readers can locate sources easily. Incorrect formatting can lead to (1) delays in the review process because editors may ask for revisions, and (2) damage to the author’s credibility, as reviewers may view the work as careless or suspect plagiarism.

data.recap: Citing sources lets you give credit, show trustworthiness, and avoid plagiarism. Different referencing styles (APA, MLA, Harvard) dictate how in‑text citations and reference lists look. Use direct quotes, paraphrases, or summaries with the appropriate citation format, and follow special rules for multiple authors, missing dates, etc. Finally, check that every citation matches a reference entry.

key_terms.meaning: A brief note in the text that points to a full source description in the reference list.
A short reference placed inside a sentence showing where an idea or quote came from.
A list at the end of a work giving full details of all sources cited.
Restating someone else's idea in your own words while keeping the meaning.
Condensing the main points of a source into a brief overview in your own words.
Latin abbreviation meaning "and others", used when a source has three or more authors.
Formatting style where the first line of a reference is flush left and subsequent lines are indented.
Using someone else's work or ideas without giving proper credit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to include citations in academic writing?
options: It gives credit and shows trustworthiness
It hides the author's own ideas
quiz.why: Citations acknowledge sources and let readers verify information.

quiz.q: Which in‑text citation style uses author‑date format?
quiz.why: APA (and Harvard) use author‑date citations.

quiz.q: How should you cite a work with four authors in APA after the first citation?
options: List all four names each time
List the first author followed by et al.
Use the title instead of authors
quiz.why: APA uses first author + et al. for three or more authors.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to format a reference list entry for a book in APA?
options: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of book. Publisher.
Title of book – Author, Year, Publisher
quiz.why: APA requires author, year, italic title, then publisher.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a summary?
options: Copying a sentence word‑for‑word with quotation marks
Restating the main ideas of a paragraph in fewer words
Changing a few words but keeping the original sentence structure
Listing the page numbers of a source
quiz.why: A summary condenses the main points in your own words.

quiz.q: What does a hanging indent look like in a reference list?
options: All lines start at the left margin
First line indented, rest flush left
First line flush left, subsequent lines indented
quiz.why: A hanging indent has the first line flush left and later lines indented.

flashcards.back: A brief note in the text that points to a full source description.
Short reference inside a sentence showing the source of an idea or quote.
Full details of every source cited, placed at the end of the work.
Restating an idea in your own words while keeping the original meaning.
A concise restatement of the main points of a source.
Latin for "and others"; used when a source has three or more authors.

data.summary: In this lesson students learn what actions count as plagiarism and how to paraphrase sources correctly. They will practice turning information into their own words while giving proper credit.
objectives: Identify different forms of plagiarism
Explain why proper citation matters
